findings.text: Hardware VLAN acceleration keeps protocol and tag control in packet metadata. One helper stores both fields. Another helper inserts the stored tag into packet bytes and then clears acceleration state, propagating a null packet on insertion failure.

Tag retrieval reports absence with a negative no-data status. The inline form first validates the embedded header protocol and otherwise returns the decoded tag. The accelerated form checks a presence flag, zeroes the output on absence, and a dispatcher selects between them based on device transmit capability.
VLAN parse result carries a network-order protocol value together with a header depth count.

Protocol discovery passes non-VLAN types through and reports MAC length as depth. For VLAN types it delegates to a deeper offset resolver and only reports depth when a nonzero protocol results. Wrappers fix the starting offset at zero, use either packet protocol or caller type, and one wrapper fails closed by returning zero when required bytes cannot be pulled.

Packet protocol selection returns the accelerated protocol when present else the base protocol, unless the caller requests VLAN skipping, in which case stacked tags are resolved to the inner protocol.

Encapsulation protocol assignment preserves recognized 802.3 EtherTypes. For other values it inspects the following word: an all-ones pattern selects 802.3 framing while remaining values select 802.2 LLC framing.
Tag removal reads tag control at Ethernet header length, refreshes the encapsulation protocol, strips one tag length from packet data, and shifts the MAC addresses forward over the gap.
Post-pull data movement warns once when the moved length exceeds the signed maximum, then delegates to the generic data move operation.

Single-tag detection is true when an accelerated tag is present or the base protocol denotes VLAN. Multi-tag detection additionally requires a second VLAN protocol after the first, handling accelerated versus inline first tags and requiring sufficient pulled header bytes for the inline case.

Feature checking leaves singly tagged packets unchanged. For multiply tagged packets it narrows device features to a small offload subset so checksum offload remains only where hardware checksum is supported.

VLAN header comparison yields zero exactly when both tag control and encapsulated protocol match. It uses a single word exclusive-or where efficient unaligned access is available, otherwise field-wise exclusive-or combined with inclusive-or.

A packet tag exists either inline in packet bytes or accelerated in metadata. Helpers move between those representations by insertion plus clear or by extraction plus store, while predicates distinguish untagged, singly tagged, and multiply tagged states.

When measurement support is disabled, command-line parsing, kexec hooks, and buffer hooks are no-ops, policy lookup returns null, appraisal enable and signature checks report negative, current hash reports a last sentinel, file and inode hashing report unsupported operation, and critical-data measurement reports missing entry.
Transport port offset is zero for TCP, UDP, DCCP, ESP, SCTP and UDPLITE, four for AH, and negative invalid for all other protocol numbers.

IPv4 classifiers test network-order addresses for loopback, multicast, local multicast, limited broadcast, all-snoopers group, zero network, private 10, 172.16, and 192.168 ranges, link-local 169.254, 6to4 anycast, and documentation ranges in 192.0.2 and 198.18 space.
Generic IPv6-capable socket address holds a family field followed by opaque bytes sized so the whole object matches an IPv6 socket address.

IPv6 well-known initializers: unspecified is all zero; loopback is all zero except final byte one; link-local, interface-local and site-local multicast groups use a leading all-ones byte, a scope byte, zero middle bytes, and a final byte of one for all-nodes or two for all-routers.
Textual address limits are sixteen characters for IPv4 and forty eight for IPv6.

Indirect-call wrappers select between optimized and plain modes. The optimized mode compares the function pointer against known targets with a likely hint and calls the matching target directly, chaining to lower arities on mismatch. The plain mode always performs an ordinary indirect call. Declaration, scope, and symbol-export helpers differ accordingly between modes.

Internet-protocol dispatch macros choose two-target, one-target, or plain indirect behavior across three variants, while the single-target family chooses between direct-compare and plain indirect behavior across two variants.
Diagnostic handler pairs an owner module with callbacks for bulk dump, single dump, info fill, auxiliary fill, and destroy, plus a diagnostic type and info size.

Diagnostic dump state holds a request attribute table with named slots for bytecode and socket storage filters, a storage diagnostic pointer, and flags recording whether mark, control-group, and user-lock filtering are needed.
Diagnostic attribute sizing sums netlink space for shutdown, service type, optional IPv6 class and single-stack flags, mark, class identifier, optional control-group identifier, and socket options.
Input event value carries a type, code, and signed measurement. Clock selection orders real, monotonic, and boot clocks with a maximum sentinel.

Input device descriptor combines identity strings and identifier, property and capability bitmaps, keymap state and operations, force-feedback and poller links, repeat and timer state, multitouch and absolute state, current key and indicator state, open and event operations, an RCU grab pointer, synchronization members, user and lifecycle flags, embedded generic device, list links, event batch buffer, management flag, and per-clock timestamps. A container helper derives the descriptor from the embedded device.
Input device event path is guarded by a spinlock while device membership operations use a mutex. Force-feedback effect management is separately serialized by its own mutex.

Input handler holds private data, single and batched event hooks, filter, match, connect, disconnect and start hooks, observer and minor metadata, name, identifier table, and list links. An input handle binds one device to one handler with private data, open count, name, batched dispatch entry, and device and handler list links.

Event reporting helpers forward key, relative, absolute, force-feedback status, switch, frame sync, and multitouch sync reports to central dispatch, normalizing key and switch values to boolean form and using fixed sync report kinds.

Device reference helpers tolerate null and delegate to generic device reference counting. Driver data helpers delegate to generic device driver storage. A packet-size hint setter records the expected events per packet.
Absolute-axis accessor generation produces a getter returning zero when axis storage is absent and a setter that ensures axis storage exists before assigning the requested field.

Force-feedback device groups upload, erase, playback, gain, autocenter, destroy and stop operations with private data, a capability bitmap, a mutex, a maximum effect count, an effect table, and a trailing owner table sized by that count.

Input attachment progresses through handler matching, connection with an open handle, optional grabbing, repeated event delivery, and disconnection, while device flags track user count, removal, inhibition, and readiness.

Multitouch axis range spans from touch major to tool vertical. Device identity matching combines bus, vendor and product, optionally with version. Tracking identifiers are bounded by hexadecimal FFFF. Multitouch mode flags occupy successive low bits for pointer, direct, drop-unused, tracking, semi-multitouch, and total-force behavior.
Multitouch slot stores one value per multitouch axis over the defined range, plus a frame counter and a tracking key.

Tag stripping assumes a tag header at a fixed offset and callers must guarantee header presence. Multi-tag and protocol-with-depth paths fail closed on short packets by reporting absent or zero. Absolute getters must tolerate missing axis storage.
